title: Looking for Comedy in the Muslim World
full_review:
By the sound of it, you might think comedian Albert Brooks is treading on politically incorrect ice with his latest movie.

But not to worry. "Looking for Comedy in the Muslim World" (Warner Independent) -- which he both wrote and directed -- is an amiable but low-key satire with a good message about America's cultural myopia and the importance of humor as a pacifier after the events of Sept. 11, 2001. And it's set in India and (briefly) Pakistan, rather than the more volatile Middle East.

Brooks plays himself at the time of a career lull. He hopes to land the James Stewart part in a revival of "Harvey," but in a funny early scene crusty director Penny Marshall (as herself) disabuses him of that notion and sends him packing.

He's in the doldrums until he receives a missive from Washington asking him to a meeting about a government mission. His eBay-addicted wife (Amy Ryan) encourages him to go. There, he learns from former U.S. Sen. (and sometime actor) Fred Dalton Thompson that he has the chance to travel abroad and learn what makes Muslims laugh.
There's no pay, beyond expenses, but hints of a Medal of Freedom in Brooks' future sweeten the proposition.

With the aid of two government handlers, Stuart (John Carroll Lynch) and Mark (Jon Tenney), he makes the long journey to Delhi, India, by coach. Agent Mark finds him a dilapidated office, and after interviewing a number of singularly unpromising candidates he hires a secretary named Maya (Sheetal Sheth), an eager young lady anxious to help.

Hanging gloomily over Brooks' head is the 500-page report he must submit at the end.
Random street polling yields few results, but eventually Brooks hatches a scheme to give a comedy improv concert to which he'll invite English-speaking Muslims. Brooks does an amusing act, but fails to elicit more than polite applause.

Red tape prevents his planned trip to Pakistan, but the agents contrive a brief illegal border crossing to that country with comic consequences.

As Brooks sincerely goes about his assigned task, he nearly causes an international incident with Pakistan.

Brooks' brand of laid-back and understated humor and the exoticism of the Delhi settings make for pleasant viewing, along with his gently satiric spin on the present-day politics and tensions often arising over inconsequential misunderstandings.

There's no racial caricaturing to speak of, notwithstanding some Pakistani comedians set up at first to look like terrorists, and present-day Indian culture is not stereotyped.
Brooks' character encounters some mildly patronizing anti-Semitism at a couple of junctures, as when he visits the office of Al-Jazeera, where officials enthusiastically pitch him the idea of starring in a sitcom with the unpromising title of "That Darn Jew." (Brooks politely declines.)

Brooks' premise is a worthy one, and who's to say the punch line might not be mightier than the sword?

The film contains a few instances of profane, rough and crude words making this best for older adolescents and up. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
